ST-020.title: Furnaces
ST-020.summary: The house feels cold, the furnace sounds different or you are planning a change. Find the repair, replacement or care path that fits what is happening.
ST-020.answer: A furnace heats air for the home. This page helps choose repair, planned replacement or care.

sections.body: Tell us whether heat stopped, a room stays cold or you want to plan ahead. The equipment type, controls and past work can help guide the right assessment.

faqs.question: How does HVAC financing work?
faqs.answer: Financing lets you repay an approved heating or cooling project over time. You still need to compare the full project price, what you will borrow, and the lender’s terms. Financing adds a payment obligation and may add interest or fees.

faqs.question: Which financing providers should I ask about?
faqs.answer: You can apply online through Synchrony, or ask MGI about Wells Fargo and Service Finance. Confirm which plans are available for your project. The lender determines approval and the terms offered to you.

faqs.question: When should I apply?
faqs.answer: Start with the equipment options and full project price. Ask MGI which financing plans apply to your project, then review the lender’s terms and application requirements before applying.

faqs.question: Does a lower monthly payment mean a lower cost?
faqs.answer: No. A longer repayment period can lower the monthly payment while increasing the total interest you pay. Compare the full repayment cost, not just the payment amount.

faqs.question: What if a plan says “no interest if paid in full”?
faqs.answer: Check whether it is a deferred-interest offer. With deferred interest, missing the payoff deadline can mean owing interest from the purchase date. Minimum payments may not pay off the balance in time. Read the actual offer before signing.

faqs.question: Is financing approval guaranteed?
faqs.answer: No. Approval and the amount available depend on the lender’s requirements. Ask how the application affects your credit before submitting it.

faqs.question: Can I pay upfront or use a rebate?
faqs.answer: Ask MGI about other payment arrangements if you prefer to pay upfront or financing is not approved. A possible rebate is separate from the loan. Keep the full project price in your budget until any rebate is confirmed.

ST-051.title: Weak cooling, ice or water? Start with the symptom.
ST-051.summary: An air conditioner can stop cooling for different reasons. Ice does not prove one failed part, and a wet area does not by itself prove a refrigerant leak.
ST-051.answer: An air conditioner can stop cooling for different reasons. Ice does not prove one failed part, and a wet area does not by itself prove a refrigerant leak.

sections.heading: Describe what changed, not which part you think failed
sections.body: Start with the change you can describe: the house is not reaching the setting, the air feels warm, water appeared or ice is visible. Then add when it began and whether it affects the whole home or one room. Those details help separate different questions. For example, “the back bedroom gets hot each afternoon” is a different starting point from “no room is cooling today.” Neither description proves a cause. You do not need to know the name of a part to ask for help. If you have a past service record or a visible display code, keep it available without opening equipment.

sections.heading: A running fan does not prove that cooling is working
sections.body: The indoor fan can move air while the equipment is not actively cooling. A fan set to On can continue moving air between cooling cycles, so air from a vent may feel different during that time. Record the thermostat mode, fan setting and room temperature shown on the display. Do not use the sound of a fan as proof that every part is operating correctly. A useful description might be, “air keeps moving, but the house has stayed above the setting.” Ask a qualified person to connect that observation to the controls, airflow, electrical supply and equipment findings.

sections.heading: Ice tells you to seek a cause, not buy a part
sections.body: The indoor coil takes heat from the home. Too little airflow and refrigerant problems can both lead to ice there, which is why the same visible symptom can have different repair paths. Stop cooling and arrange a qualified check rather than using thawing as proof that the issue is solved. Tell the service team where the ice was visible and whether cooling or airflow changed before it appeared. Keep refrigerant work and internal checks with a qualified person. Repeatedly treating the ice without establishing its cause leaves the original question unanswered and makes it hard to compare repair recommendations.

sections.heading: Separate visible water from a refrigerant question
sections.body: Water near an air conditioner is an observation, not proof that refrigerant is leaking. Describe the location without reaching inside the equipment: beneath the indoor unit, near a drain or somewhere else. Note whether it appears only while cooling runs and whether an error appeared at the same time. The useful next step is a check that identifies the source and the affected work. Ask the technician to distinguish what was confirmed from what remains uncertain. A proposal should explain the specific repair rather than grouping every wet area under the same broad leak label.

sections.heading: Compare repair with replacement on the actual finding
sections.body: Weak cooling does not automatically require a new air conditioner. Ask what was checked, what caused the problem, which work is proposed and what that work is expected to address. Then compare parts availability, equipment condition, warranty and the total repair with a complete replacement if replacement is a viable choice. The refrigerant type can affect a repair discussion, but the R-22 phaseout alone does not require replacing an existing unit. EPA’s guidance distinguishes a regulatory change from your actual equipment decision. Availability and cost still need checking before either path becomes a sound recommendation.

sections.heading: Keep a room problem visible after a repair
sections.body: Imagine that a repaired part allows the AC to run again, but a back room still feels hot. This is a hypothetical decision example, not an MGI job. Restoring operation does not by itself show that the room concern has been addressed. Keep the original room, timing and pattern in the conversation. Ask whether the finding explains both concerns or whether the room needs a separate check. A larger outdoor unit is not a conclusion supported by a room description alone. The right comparison follows what has been checked and what the proposed work can actually change.

sections.heading: Before arranging the next step
sections.body: For a current loss of cooling, ask about a repair assessment. For equipment that still works while you compare future choices, ask about a planned replacement conversation instead. Share the address, main symptom, when it changed and one way to reach you. Confirm whether the requested work and address can be served, what the visit covers, any charges and current availability. You do not need a model number before asking. A request is not an appointment. Keep the original concern so any later findings can be compared with what you first noticed.

sections.heading: Ask for the finding in language you can use
sections.body: A repair explanation should connect the observation to the proposed work. Ask, “What did you check, what did it show and what would this repair change?” If the answer depends on a part that has not been checked, keep that uncertainty visible. If an estimate changes after further investigation, compare the new finding and work rather than treating the earlier number as a complete promise. Keep the repair’s intended result separate from unrelated upgrades. You should be able to describe the reason for the next step without learning every part name or assuming that every symptom comes from the same cause.

sections.heading: Use a symptom note you can share
sections.body: Keep a short note with four parts: what changed, where you noticed it, when it happens and what the display shows. For a hypothetical example: “The living room and bedroom both stay warm. It began yesterday afternoon. Air is moving, but I have not seen the room temperature fall. The thermostat is set to cooling.” That supplies a useful starting point without naming a failed component. If the next question is about water or ice, describe it separately rather than changing the whole note into a leak diagnosis. Later, ask which observation the findings explain and which remains unanswered. Keep this note for the repair discussion so the proposed result can be compared with the original concern, even if a different person handles the next conversation.

ST-052.title: Check the program before counting the rebate.
ST-052.summary: Colorado heat-pump incentives can have different account, equipment, contractor and timing conditions. Confirm the current official rules for the actual project.
ST-052.answer: Colorado heat-pump incentives can have different account, equipment, contractor and timing conditions. Confirm the current official rules for the actual project.

sections.heading: Do not count the former federal credit in a new 2026 project
sections.body: The IRS’s current Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit page says the Section 25C credit applies to qualifying improvements made through December 31, 2025. Do not count that former credit toward a new 2026 installation. Filing a return in 2026 for qualifying work from 2025 is a different question. Ask a qualified tax advisor about your actual year and circumstances, and check the current IRS guidance rather than an older equipment or incentive page.

sections.heading: Why the account matters more than the town name
sections.body: Two homes with similar mailing addresses can have different utility accounts. A town or ZIP code is a useful location clue, but it does not establish the program that applies. Start with the actual electric bill and, where relevant, the gas bill. Keep the providers separate when a project changes the fuel used for heating. Then match those accounts to the current official program. This helps avoid comparing a proposal using a payment intended for another utility territory. Share account-provider information only when it is useful for the check; a general inquiry does not need payment details or private financial records.

sections.heading: Ask which project the program is evaluating
sections.body: A heat pump that heats and cools rooms is different from a heat-pump water heater. The latter warms stored water and has its own equipment and installation questions. A broad heat-pump heading does not mean one set of rules covers both. Identify the exact proposed model, what it replaces, the existing fuel and the work included. Ask whether the program evaluates the equipment alone or requires other project records. A different model or installation plan can change the answer, so keep the checked version with the proposal rather than relying on a general product-family label.

sections.heading: Put the timing questions before authorization
sections.body: Some programs have conditions that must be met before work starts. Others ask for documents after completion, with their own deadlines. Before approving a project, ask whether it needs preapproval, a reservation or a qualifying installer. Make clear who submits each item and who keeps the confirmation. Do not assume a contractor’s quote is itself a program approval. If a rule uses a purchase date and another uses a completion date, ask the program which clock applies to the actual application. Avoid relying on a deadline copied from an old promotion or a different utility’s page.

sections.heading: Use a short record for each possible program
sections.body: Keep one record per program with the official name and source, date checked, project and account conditions, required documents, next action and person responsible. Record what has been confirmed and what remains open. For example, the equipment might be listed while installer participation still needs checking. That is a partial check, not an award. If several programs are being considered, keep their records separate so the rules are not blended together. Use this as a planning checklist. Ask who handles each application and which records you need to keep.

sections.heading: Do not add headline amounts without checking the combination
sections.body: Two programs may each describe a possible payment, but that does not establish that the same project can receive both. Ask whether the programs allow combining benefits, whether a cost cap applies and whether one payment changes another calculation. The word “up to” names a limit, not your approved amount. Funding and the actual project conditions can also affect the answer. Keep a combined estimate marked as conditional until the relevant checks are complete. A larger headline is not useful if the proposed equipment, installer or timing fails a condition that was left out of the comparison.

sections.heading: Compare the amount due with a possible later payment
sections.body: Keep three figures distinct: the full project price, what is due under the agreed terms and any possible payment from a program later. A possible rebate is not necessarily cash available on installation day. Ask how the payment is issued and who receives it. Financing is another separate decision, with its own approval and borrowing terms. If a quote shows only a price after a possible incentive, ask for the full price and assumptions too. You should be able to judge the commitment even while the program answer is still open, without treating an estimate as money received.

sections.heading: Keep equipment fit and tax questions separate
sections.body: An incentive can help a project comparison, but it cannot establish that a particular model fits the home. Heating needs, cold-weather performance and installation work still need a qualified check. A tax benefit also differs from a utility payment. Ask a qualified tax advisor about the applicable year and your circumstances, rather than treating an equipment quote as tax advice. For the next conversation, bring the actual providers, proposed model and timing question. Ask what has been verified against the official rules and what still needs an answer. This guide does not qualify a household or promise an amount.

sections.heading: Give each open requirement an owner
sections.body: Before counting on a program, name the next unanswered requirement and who will check it. One person may need to confirm equipment listing while another asks the program about installer participation or timing. Keep the reply with the relevant source and date so an old answer is not applied to a changed project. If work must wait for a program decision, make that dependency clear before agreeing to timing. If you choose to proceed without counting the benefit, keep that choice explicit too. A homeowner should not have to infer who submits documents or assume that a pending application will be accepted.

sections.heading: Read the project record before gathering documents
sections.body: Use the proposed model and itemized work to identify which records a program may need. A model identifier, invoice, equipment certificate or installation record can serve different purposes; ask the official program what is required before assuming they are interchangeable. Do not send private payment or financial information with a broad equipment inquiry. If the installer or model changes, check whether that affects the earlier answer. Keep the version of the proposal that was reviewed and the reply from the program together. This helps separate an equipment check from a completed application and preserves the basis for the comparison if the project changes. Required documents, their recipient and the person submitting them should be clear before a pending step is treated as complete.

faqs.question: Can I combine incentives?
faqs.answer: Only if the current programs permit it. Check whether the programs can be combined, whether funding is available and which documents the actual project needs.

faqs.question: Can an estimate promise my rebate?
faqs.answer: No. Eligibility, approval and payment belong to the program’s current process. Keep a possible amount separate from the price and amount due.

ST-053.title: A heat pump may fit. Start with the home.
ST-053.summary: A space heat pump can heat and cool. The right choice depends on the home’s heating needs, cold-weather output, installation scope and actual energy prices.
ST-053.answer: A space heat pump can heat and cool. The right choice depends on the home’s heating needs, cold-weather output, installation scope and actual energy prices.

sections.heading: Understand the equipment before choosing the offer
sections.body: A heat pump for rooms moves heat into the home for heating and out of the home for cooling. A heat-pump water heater instead uses heat from surrounding air to warm stored water. Start by naming which need you are exploring. If the question began with a cold room, a stopped system or a higher bill, say so. The same technology label does not make those problems identical. Existing equipment that has failed needs a service assessment; curiosity about a future fuel change can follow a planning conversation. Keep the current need visible before comparing new equipment or possible incentives.

sections.heading: Ask how much heat the home needs
sections.body: A heat pump’s advertised output must be compared with the home it will serve. ENERGY STAR advises a calculation of the home’s heating and cooling needs, commonly called Manual J, before equipment is sized. Ask what information and local conditions were used and which rooms the proposal covers. A floor-area shortcut or the size of the existing unit does not explain the whole recommendation. ACCA’s equipment-selection guidance connects home needs, design conditions and manufacturer performance data. The practical question is simple: “What shows that this model can supply the heat my home needs under the conditions used in the plan?”

sections.heading: Read a cold-weather claim in context
sections.body: A model’s lowest operating temperature tells you something about whether it can run, but not whether it supplies enough heat for your home at that temperature. A cold-climate designation includes tested performance requirements. It remains necessary to compare the exact model’s cold-weather output with the home’s need. Ask for the performance information behind the proposed design, rather than a claim based only on the label. Keep the model and equipment combination clear. A broad statement about heat pumps in Colorado cannot replace a home-specific comparison or show how a particular installation will behave in every room.

sections.heading: Make backup heat part of the plan
sections.body: A heat pump may be considered with a furnace, a combination often called dual fuel, or in a design using electricity alone. Ask what supplies backup heat, when it is used and how the controls choose between sources. Keep the proposed settings and equipment match in the explanation. Homes can need different backup arrangements. Ask which designs are available for your equipment and home. A useful proposal makes the actual plan visible. If electrical work or another trade is needed, ask who performs it, who arranges it and whether its cost is included before comparing the totals.

sections.heading: Compare efficiency with running costs carefully
sections.body: An equipment rating is measured under a defined test method. It is useful for comparing equipment, but it is not your household bill. Running-cost estimates also need current electricity and fuel prices, the proposed model’s performance and expected use. Ask which assumptions the comparison uses and which changes would affect it. Keep the full installation price and borrowing cost separate from estimated running costs. If someone describes a payback period, ask what evidence supports that calculation. A higher rating alone does not establish lower bills, a guaranteed saving or a date on which the project pays for itself.

sections.heading: Keep room goals in the equipment comparison
sections.body: Imagine a homeowner considering a heat pump because the back room never feels right. This is a hypothetical planning example, not a completed project. The proposal should explain whether the reported pattern has been checked and what the equipment change is expected to address. Ask what might remain after replacement. A change in technology does not, by itself, establish that every room concern disappears. If one room needs a separate investigation, keep that question assigned rather than hiding it inside a whole-home comfort claim. The useful result of the first conversation may be another check before a model is selected.

sections.heading: Bring the question that started the search
sections.body: For a planning inquiry, describe the equipment you have if known, the rooms involved, the concern you want addressed and any timing needs. Ask about the assessment’s purpose, charges, address coverage and availability before arranging it. You can also request an explanation of what would stay and what would change, including controls and other work. Check potential incentives against current official conditions after the actual project is defined. Leave the conversation knowing which comparison is ready and which questions remain. A request is not an appointment, and you can take time to compare the choices without treating a general article as a recommendation for your home.

sections.heading: See what stays and what changes
sections.body: A replacement conversation should identify the equipment and controls that remain, not only the new outdoor unit. Ask whether the proposed pieces are approved to work together and which checks confirm operation after installation. Those setup and operating checks are often called commissioning. Keep any electrical or other-trade task, responsible party and cost inclusion clear. If a proposal leaves one of those items open, ask how it affects the full price and timing. This makes two options easier to compare without assuming that changing technology means replacing every component, or that the price of one new unit covers all the work.

sections.heading: Separate performance, price and your priorities
sections.body: Consider a hypothetical household comparing two suitable heat-pump proposals. One has a higher efficiency rating, while the other includes different electrical or control work. The rating alone cannot tell them which finished project fits their priorities. Write down the questions that matter: the rooms served, cold-weather output, backup arrangement, included installation work, full price and open costs. Ask which differences change operation and which change the commitment. If the current concern is an unexpectedly high bill, compare the prices and use behind that bill before assuming new equipment solves it. This example does not rank models or predict savings. It shows how a clear project record can keep a technology choice connected to the concern that started it.

ST-054.title: Furnace will not start? Put safety first.
ST-054.summary: If you smell gas, leave the building and call 911 or the gas utility from a safe place. If you suspect carbon monoxide, move outside to fresh air immediately and call 911. For a loss of heat without immediate danger, describe the symptom and ask about service availability.
ST-054.answer: If you smell gas, leave the building and call 911 or the gas utility from a safe place. If you suspect carbon monoxide, move outside to fresh air immediately and call 911. For a loss of heat without immediate danger, describe the symptom and ask about service availability.

sections.heading: Notice the sequence without opening the furnace
sections.body: A clear sequence helps more than a guessed part name. Does the furnace stay silent, begin briefly and stop, or keep moving air without warming the house? Note the thermostat’s displayed temperature and selected mode, any visible error and the time the change began. If you hear a new sound, describe when it occurs rather than trying to find it inside the equipment. You can ask for service without providing all these details. The point is to give the assessment a starting place, not make the homeowner responsible for diagnosing gas, electrical or internal equipment problems.

sections.heading: Keep immediate danger separate from a service request
sections.body: A gas smell or suspected carbon-monoxide problem is not a reason to wait for a reply to a website form. For a gas smell, leave the building and call 911 or the gas utility from a safe place. Do not operate switches or attempt to relight the furnace. If you suspect carbon monoxide, move outside to fresh air immediately and call 911. A furnace-service request is for the equipment conversation after safety has been addressed; it does not confirm emergency dispatch. If there is no immediate danger but the heat has stopped, ask about service availability. No article can determine whether your equipment is safe to run.

sections.heading: A display is an observation, not a complete diagnosis
sections.body: A thermostat that shows a temperature or an error can supply useful information. It does not prove that the furnace has power, that its controls are working correctly or that fuel is being burned safely. Read the normal display without removing covers. Tell the service team what mode is selected and whether the room temperature changes. If the display is blank, say that rather than assuming the furnace itself has failed. Different models use different error information, so keep the exact code if one is visible. The model instructions and qualified checks determine what the information means.

sections.heading: Airflow can be part of a heating problem
sections.body: Carrier’s furnace guidance describes restricted airflow as a possible contributor to shutdowns. A clogged filter or blocked register can be involved, but that does not establish the cause in your home. If a filter service record is available, share it. Follow the equipment’s owner instructions for ordinary care, and keep internal checks with a qualified person. Ask whether the assessment found an airflow issue, a control issue or another fault, and how the finding was supported. Replacing a filter does not by itself prove that a repeated shutdown or an unexplained room problem is resolved.

sections.heading: Short starts need an explanation before repeated resets
sections.body: A furnace that starts and stops repeatedly presents a different pattern from one that never starts. Describe how often you notice it and whether the home warms between starts. A loud bang at ignition needs professional attention rather than repeated attempts to make the furnace run. Do not relight equipment, open internal panels or treat repeated resets as the repair. Ask the technician what was observed, which checks support the cause and what remains uncertain. A stopped or cycling furnace does not tell you, by itself, whether the next choice should be repair, further assessment or replacement.

sections.heading: Ask what the repair would address
sections.body: When a fault is found, ask for the work in plain words: which part or condition needs attention, why that action fits the finding and what is included in the price. Keep the current failure separate from optional improvements. Ask whether parts are available, what the warranty covers and how any unresolved issue changes the plan. If replacement is also discussed, compare a complete installation with the actual repair rather than comparing a small part price with an equipment-only price. Age alone does not supply the missing evidence or show that the repair cannot be a sound choice.

sections.heading: Keep the original concern for the result check
sections.body: Imagine a furnace that begins running after repair while a back bedroom remains cold. This is a hypothetical example. It shows why “the furnace starts” and “the room concern was addressed” can be different questions. Describe both concerns at the start so the findings can explain which one the work addresses. Ask what was checked after repair and what you should notice if the issue returns. Do not assume that one successful start proves lasting performance under every condition. A useful completion explanation identifies the work done, its observed result and anything that remains open.

sections.heading: Prepare a small, useful service request
sections.body: Share the address, what stopped, when it changed and how to reach you. A model number, technical diagnosis or photograph is not a prerequisite for asking about help. Confirm whether the work and address can be served, the assessment’s purpose, any charges and available scheduling. If no visit can be offered, ask what that means for the request rather than assuming someone is on the way. An appointment needs a separate confirmation. Use these details to understand the conversation you need, not as proof that a visit has been arranged.

sections.heading: Give two patterns separate places in the conversation
sections.body: A hypothetical homeowner might report that the furnace has stopped today and that one room has been cold for months. Keep the immediate failure and the longer pattern separate when asking for service. The first question is what stopped the furnace. The second is whether that finding explains the room as well. Neither description proves the cause. A technician may establish a supported repair while the room question still needs attention. Ask for that distinction in the explanation rather than treating a successful restart as the answer to both concerns. Record any unresolved room or recurring-start question with the proposed next check. You can make that request in ordinary words without assigning yourself a technical diagnosis or requiring a larger replacement.

faqs.question: What if I smell gas or suspect carbon monoxide?
faqs.answer: For a gas smell, leave the building and call 911 or the gas utility from a safe place. Do not operate switches or attempt to relight equipment. If you suspect carbon monoxide, move outside to fresh air immediately and call 911. Do not wait for an HVAC request.

faqs.question: Should I replace a furnace that will not start?
faqs.answer: Not from that symptom alone. Identify the cause, repair scope and condition before comparing replacement.

ST-055.title: Repair or replace? Compare the finding and the full scope.
ST-055.summary: A furnace’s age alone does not settle the choice. Compare the cause, repair history, parts, home needs and total work involved.
ST-055.answer: A furnace’s age alone does not settle the choice. Compare the cause, repair history, parts, home needs and total work involved.

sections.heading: Start with the problem you want the decision to solve
sections.body: A furnace decision can begin with no heat, repeated trouble, a room that stays cold or a planned change while equipment still works. Name the concern before comparing quotes. A repair that restores operation may not address every room issue, and a replacement proposal should explain what it is expected to change. Write the concern in one ordinary sentence and keep it with the options. For example, “we want the furnace to stop shutting down” is clearer than “we want an upgrade.” This is a planning example, not a diagnosis or a completed MGI project.

sections.heading: Separate a finding from a guess
sections.body: A finding should explain what was observed or measured and how it supports the proposed cause. Ask which checks were completed, what they showed and whether anything still needs checking. A visible error, equipment age or repeated symptom may guide the assessment without deciding the outcome alone. If two recommendations differ, compare the evidence behind them rather than assuming one company must be wrong. A second look can clarify what has been confirmed and what remains uncertain. It does not promise a different answer, a free visit or a reason to reject properly supported work.

sections.heading: Make the repair option complete enough to compare
sections.body: Ask what the repair includes, whether the needed parts are available and which warranty terms apply. Keep the full repair price visible, including the actual listed work and any unresolved cost. Ask what the repair is expected to restore and whether it leaves another concern for a separate check. If the problem has returned before, bring the service record if available. A repeated problem deserves an explanation, but it does not establish a universal replacement rule. A useful comparison states what each path addresses instead of describing a repair only as a temporary choice or a replacement only as an upgrade.

sections.heading: Make the replacement option a whole project
sections.body: The new furnace is one part of the comparison. Ask for the proposed model, how much heat it supplies and why it fits the home’s needs. Include existing fuel connections, venting, controls and any required work by another trade. Ask what equipment stays and what changes. The proposal should identify who arranges permits and other work, whether those costs are included and what must happen before installation. An unexplained “by others” note leaves a responsibility open. Defining that work does not mean MGI performs every trade or pays every fee; the actual agreement must make the responsibilities clear.

sections.heading: Understand what the efficiency rating can tell you
sections.body: AFUE compares furnace fuel efficiency under a defined method. It does not predict the full bill for a home, since fuel prices, thermostat use and heat lost from the building affect the result. The rating also does not decide whether the furnace supplies the right amount of heat. Keep efficiency, equipment fit and the project price as related but separate questions. If a running-cost estimate is offered, ask which prices, use and performance assumptions it uses. Do not treat a higher rating as proof that a particular household will save a stated amount or recover the purchase cost by a set date.

sections.heading: Use age and repair history as context
sections.body: Age can help describe the equipment, but it does not replace a condition check. Past repairs, current findings, available parts and the home’s needs all affect a comparison. Avoid deciding from a single birthday or a fixed repair-price percentage. Ask what evidence makes a repair viable, what evidence supports replacement and which questions could change the recommendation. If the furnace still works and the project is being planned, say so. The timing conversation can differ from a current loss of heat. Neither situation authorizes invented scarcity or a claim that you must decide before understanding the work.

sections.heading: Compare money at the same level
sections.body: Put the full repair price beside the full replacement project, with inclusions and open costs shown. Keep possible incentives separate from confirmed reductions and the amount due. Financing has its own approval, fees, repayment period and borrowing cost, so a monthly payment is not the same as a project price. A rebate possibility cannot establish that the equipment fits, and a lower payment cannot establish a lower total cost. If one quote leaves other-trade work open while another includes it, resolve that difference before treating the totals as equivalent. You can ask for clarification before choosing.

sections.heading: Leave with a clear next decision
sections.body: A useful next step might be authorizing a supported repair, arranging a home assessment, comparing written options or waiting for an unresolved answer. Ask which question you need to decide now and which can wait. If proceeding with installation, ask what setup and operating checks are included and how you will learn the controls. For an inquiry, share the concern, address and relevant past work if available. Confirm assessment scope, charges and availability before treating a request as an appointment. General education cannot determine your furnace’s condition; the evidence and actual project terms govern the choice at your home.

sections.heading: Check whether two proposals answer the same question
sections.body: Consider a hypothetical comparison in which one proposal addresses a confirmed failed part and another describes a new furnace plus different controls. Those totals do not yet answer the same project question. Ask what each choice changes, what remains in place and what is excluded. Then put the unresolved room concern or repeated-failure history beside both choices. The purpose is not to force matching prices or assume a competitor has omitted work. It is to understand whether the recommendations address the same need. If the explanations use different findings, ask what check would resolve the difference before treating either price as decisive. A homeowner can compare the scope without having to guess at measurements or accept a broader project simply because it has a stronger equipment label.

faqs.question: Does the furnace age tell me whether to replace it?
faqs.answer: Age is one clue, not a decision by itself. Condition, repair history, available parts, the home’s heat needs and full project cost matter.

faqs.question: Why does the furnace start and stop so often?
faqs.answer: Restricted airflow, a control problem or equipment that is too large can be involved. The pattern needs checking before choosing a repair.

ST-056.title: Heat-pump water heaters: check the room as well as the tank.
ST-056.summary: A heat-pump water heater uses heat from surrounding air to warm stored water. Space, temperature, hot-water use and other installation work determine whether it fits.
ST-056.answer: A heat-pump water heater uses heat from surrounding air to warm stored water. Space, temperature, hot-water use and other installation work determine whether it fits.

sections.heading: A water-heating decision has its own questions
sections.body: A heat-pump water heater warms stored water using heat from surrounding air. It does not heat and cool the home in the way a room-conditioning heat pump does. Start with the hot-water question: do you run short, want to compare future options or have a current equipment fault? A planning guide is useful for fit and project questions. A current leak, loss of hot water or recurring error needs a service assessment if the service is available for your equipment. Keep the equipment’s actual model in the conversation because room requirements, controls and repair choices vary rather than following one rule for every heater.

sections.heading: Check the actual room against the model instructions
sections.body: Room dimensions alone do not establish fit. Compare the proposed model’s required air space, temperature range, clearances and access with the installation location. Objects in a room can affect available space, and a small enclosed closet cannot be assumed suitable from a generic benchmark. ENERGY STAR’s buying and technical guidance offer useful background, while the exact manufacturer instructions govern the proposed model. Ask which requirement was checked and how the installation meets it. If a different room arrangement is proposed, make its work and cost visible rather than treating it as a detail to decide after purchase.

sections.heading: Consider sound and the effect on the surrounding room
sections.body: A heat-pump water heater makes operating noise and cools the space around it while transferring heat into the water. Consider where people sleep or spend quiet time near the proposed location. Ask for the exact model’s sound information and what the placement means for that room. A general sound range cannot promise what a particular household will hear. The room’s temperature also matters to operation. Cold air or cold incoming water can increase use of the backup electric heating element. Keep those conditions in the fit discussion before assuming the technology will use the same amount of electricity in every installation.

sections.heading: Compare delivery with your busiest hot-water use
sections.body: Tank size tells you how much water can be stored, but it does not tell the whole delivery story. First-hour rating estimates how much hot water a fully heated tank can deliver during the first hour. Tell the evaluator which uses overlap, such as showers and another hot-water task, without treating that list as a sizing formula. Ask how the proposed model’s delivery and reheating fit the home’s needs. The answer also depends on operating modes and conditions. A larger tank or a familiar technology label is not, by itself, evidence that every period of heavy use will be served.

sections.heading: Understand the choices between operating modes
sections.body: The proposed model’s modes can affect how it heats water and uses backup electric heat. Ask which mode is intended for ordinary use, when another mode is needed and how a change affects performance. Keep the explanation tied to the actual model rather than assuming every control behaves the same way. If you compare running costs, include current electricity prices, expected hot-water use and the operating assumptions. An efficiency rating is a comparison tool, not a guaranteed bill. Ask what could change the estimate, particularly if the installation room or hot-water demand differs from the assumptions used.

sections.heading: Make the other installation work visible
sections.body: The project may require checks of electrical supply, drainage, water connections, permits and startup. Ask who performs each applicable task, who arranges it, who pays and whether it is included in the quote. Drainage for water collected during operation needs a planned route; access for future filter and tank care matters too. Water-heater work is separate from general plumbing. Ask who handles any plumbing or electrical task and whether the quote includes it. Keep any work outside the agreement clearly assigned before authorization. A whole-project comparison includes those responsibilities rather than making the tank price stand in for the finished installation.

sections.heading: Plan care and troubleshooting around the exact model
sections.body: Heat-pump water heaters have air-filter care as well as tank-related care. Ask where the filter is, what the model instructions require and what the visit includes. Dust and use can affect how often attention is needed. A recurring code or changed hot-water supply needs more than repeatedly clearing a reminder. Record the model and visible code without opening equipment. Some models have particular limits on compressor service, so neither one error nor a generic repair rule decides the answer. The manufacturer’s guidance, qualified checks and warranty terms determine whether the available next step is care, repair or replacement.

sections.heading: Choose the next conversation before choosing the tank
sections.body: If equipment still works, advance planning can allow time to compare models and installation needs. Ask about the assessment, actual scheduling and any charges rather than assuming a universal ordering time. Check any potential program against the utility account, exact equipment, installer and current rules. Keep the full project price visible until a benefit is confirmed. For a request, share the address, current equipment if known, hot-water concern and timing needs. Confirm capability and coverage before arranging a visit. A submitted request is not an appointment. The right first outcome may be a clear fit check rather than a purchase.

sections.heading: Read the care access into the placement choice
sections.body: During a planning conversation, ask how the proposed location allows access to the filter, tank and any drain that needs care. The clearances in the exact model instructions matter both at installation and later. A hypothetical layout might provide room for the tank but make an access point hard to reach after other items are stored nearby. Ask how the model’s required working space will remain available rather than assuming the initial fit settles every future task. Keep the answer with the proposed placement and included work. This is a design question, not advice to change plumbing or electrical equipment yourself. A useful proposal lets you understand the care access and operating conditions as well as where the new tank will stand.

faqs.question: Is this the same as a heat pump that warms the house?
faqs.answer: No. A heat-pump water heater warms stored water. A space heat pump heats and cools rooms. They have different fit and service questions.

faqs.question: Will a heat-pump water heater fit any utility room?
faqs.answer: No. Air space, temperature range, clearances, noise, water drainage and electrical supply need model-specific checks.

ST-057.title: Mini split or ducted system? Start with the rooms.
ST-057.summary: The layout, existing equipment and rooms you want to serve matter more than a technology label. Compare the complete scope and room-level limits.
ST-057.answer: The layout, existing equipment and rooms you want to serve matter more than a technology label. Compare the complete scope and room-level limits.

sections.heading: Begin with the rooms the project needs to serve
sections.body: A technology choice becomes easier when the intended rooms are clear. List where you want heating or cooling, when each room feels wrong and whether the project covers one area or the whole home. Keep a current failure separate from a planned change. A room that gets too warm each afternoon may need a different investigation from equipment that no longer starts. You do not need a floor-plan drawing to ask the first question. The useful starting point is a description of the rooms and concern, followed by a qualified check of what the proposed work could address.

sections.heading: Understand what single zone and multiple zones mean
sections.body: A single-zone ductless setup connects one indoor unit with one outdoor unit. A multiple-zone design serves several indoor units using a manufacturer-approved combination. Those descriptions explain connections; they do not prove that the chosen equipment can supply every room’s required heating and cooling at the same time. Ask which indoor unit serves each room and which outdoor equipment it pairs with. The actual combination and performance information matter. An advertised maximum number of indoor units is not a sizing recommendation for your home, and adding their labels does not establish enough whole-home output.

sections.heading: Closed doors change the room question
sections.body: One indoor unit does not necessarily heat or cool rooms behind closed doors. Describe how the home is actually used rather than assuming every doorway stays open. For a hypothetical example, a unit serving a shared living space might be proposed while a bedroom door is usually closed. Ask how the plan addresses that bedroom instead of assuming the shared-space unit covers it. This is a planning example, not an MGI project or equipment recommendation. Keep room-level limits visible so the proposal can be judged against your need rather than a broad whole-home comfort statement.

sections.heading: Compare output with the actual room needs
sections.body: Equipment choice follows the amount of heating and cooling needed, not the technology name alone. Ask what home or room calculation supports the proposal and what local conditions were used. Then compare the manufacturer’s performance data for the actual indoor and outdoor combination. For a heat pump, cold-weather output matters as well as cooling. A low advertised operating-temperature limit shows where equipment can operate; it does not establish enough heat for the rooms. Ask what output is available under the conditions used in the design and how any backup plan relates to the home’s need.

sections.heading: See where the equipment and connections will go
sections.body: A ductless proposal should make indoor-unit placement, outdoor equipment, pipe routes, drainage and control use understandable. Ask how those locations affect access for care and the intended airflow into the room. Manufacturers offer different indoor forms, such as wall-mounted and ceiling units, but availability does not establish fit in every space. Compare the actual proposed location and required work instead of selecting from a photograph alone. A ducted option also needs compatible equipment and a home-needs check. Existing ducts or equipment are context to evaluate, not proof that either choice is automatically suitable.

sections.heading: Compare the complete project and assigned work
sections.body: Put the indoor and outdoor equipment, connections, drains, controls, electrical work and operating checks into the comparison. Ask what stays, what changes and who arranges any work by another trade. Keep included and excluded costs clear. MGI does not offer duct work or duct cleaning. Ask which equipment work the proposed visit includes. If a dependency falls outside the agreement, ask who will perform and arrange it before authorization. A useful price comparison describes the finished work and unresolved responsibilities rather than putting two equipment-only totals beside each other.

sections.heading: Make controls and care part of the handoff
sections.body: Ask how you will choose heating or cooling, understand the displays and use the proposed controls. Identify each indoor unit that a care visit would include. A visit to the outdoor equipment alone is not a complete checklist for every indoor unit. Access, filter care, drainage and any deeper cleaning need an equipment-specific explanation. A lasting smell, water leak or performance change calls for a separate assessment rather than an assumption that routine cleaning solves it. Care instructions should follow the exact model, and ordinary homeowner observations should not become a tutorial for electrical or refrigerant repairs.

sections.heading: Keep an existing-system fault on the repair path
sections.body: If a mini split already serves the rooms but has stopped working, begin with the changed behavior, selected mode and visible error. Say whether one indoor unit or several are affected. A water leak and a refrigerant leak are different questions. Some heat pumps pause heating to melt ice from the outdoor coil, but persistent ice or a room that stays cold needs a qualified check. Do not chip ice from the unit. For planning or repair, confirm address coverage, the visit purpose, charges and availability. A request needs a separate appointment confirmation; it does not establish that either technology has been chosen for your home.

sections.heading: Compare two room plans on paper
sections.body: For a hypothetical choice between a ductless proposal and a ducted alternative, list the rooms served by each and mark which doors are normally closed. Beside each room, record the proposed equipment, intended heating and cooling role, control location and any stated limit. Keep outdoor equipment, electrical work, pipes or drains and work by another trade in a separate project list. Ask which items the price includes and what remains unresolved. This is a comparison tool, not a sizing calculation or a recommendation for either technology. It helps reveal whether one quote describes the whole home while another covers only selected rooms. Resolve that difference before using the totals or the number of indoor units to choose.

faqs.question: Will one indoor unit serve every room?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Closed doors and the layout change how air moves. Plan for the actual rooms rather than assuming one indoor unit covers the whole home.

faqs.question: Is a pause in heating always a fault?
faqs.answer: Some heat pumps pause heating while melting ice from the outdoor coil, a cycle called defrost. Ice that stays, an error or a room that stays cold needs a qualified check; do not chip ice off the unit.

ST-058.title: Dust, dryness or stale air? Describe the pattern first.
ST-058.summary: An air concern is not a diagnosis. What you notice, where it happens and when it changes can help identify a useful next check.
ST-058.answer: An air concern is not a diagnosis. What you notice, where it happens and when it changes can help identify a useful next check.

sections.heading: Name the concern in ordinary words
sections.body: Start with what you notice: dust returns quickly, a room smells stale, the air feels dry or moisture appears in a particular place. Add where it happens, when it changes and any visible source you can describe. Keep those observations separate rather than grouping everything under bad air. They lead to different questions and do not identify a pollutant or medical cause on their own. You do not need to buy a monitor or name a treatment before asking for help. A useful first conversation narrows the concern and explains which assessment, if any, can address it.

sections.heading: A pattern can guide a check without proving the cause
sections.body: Record the room and timing without turning the observation into a diagnosis. For a hypothetical example, an odor noticed after a particular household activity gives the evaluator a different starting point from moisture that stays visible in one location. Neither pattern proves a cause or shows that a product is needed. Ask how the assessment will use the description and what it can establish. If the question belongs to a specialist outside the services MGI provides, keep that limit clear. An indoor-air service discussion does not offer medical diagnosis, mold treatment or every kind of building investigation.

sections.heading: Removing a source and cleaning air do different jobs
sections.body: EPA prioritizes reducing or removing pollution sources and bringing in clean outdoor air, with filtration as a supporting approach. Ask whether a possible action addresses the source, air exchange or particles already in the air. Those are related but different jobs. A filter may be relevant to some airborne particles without resolving the condition that produces them. Source control is a general principle, not an MGI offer of every task it might require. Keep the proposed work bounded and name any outside specialist or separate action only where verified. Avoid choosing one device as the automatic answer to every concern.

sections.heading: Check outside conditions before using ventilation
sections.body: Opening a window can change air exchange, but outdoor air is not always the right answer. Check current conditions, including smoke alerts, before relying on outside air. EPA’s smoke guidance includes cleaner-air rooms and suitable filtration while preserving heat safety and emergency directions. A seasonal or regional air concern does not establish the conditions at your home today. The question is whether the proposed action is appropriate for the current situation. Do not treat a ventilation suggestion as a guarantee of safe air, or allow a product discussion to delay evacuation or urgent help when the situation calls for it.

sections.heading: Match a particle filter to the equipment
sections.body: Filters have different ratings and fit requirements. For smoke, EPA recommends MERV 13 or higher central filtration where the equipment can support it. MERV is a rating used to compare particle capture; a higher number is not automatically suitable for every system. Ask whether the proposed filter fits the equipment and allows the required airflow. The actual model and installation matter. Portable air cleaners instead need a comparison with the room they will serve. Keep their smoke clean-air delivery rate, room size and manufacturer instructions together rather than assuming a small unit treats every part of a home.

sections.heading: Keep particles, gases and moisture separate
sections.body: A particle filter targets airborne particles. Gas removal uses different material and has its own limits. Moisture raises another set of questions about the actual conditions and possible sources. A product described as an air purifier does not prove equal performance for all three concerns. Ask which pollutant the product addresses, what evidence supports that use and what remains outside its reach. Consider airflow, room size, fit, filter replacement, sound and information about ozone or other substances. Air cleaners and HVAC filters cannot remove every pollutant, and a laboratory result does not establish the same result throughout a home.

sections.heading: Understand what a measurement can and cannot show
sections.body: A brief reading from one device in one place does not describe every pollutant in the home. Ask what the device measures, its limits, where it was used, for how long and under which conditions. Keep measured observations separate from a possible source or a confirmed finding. If a follow-up check is proposed, ask which unanswered question it will address and whether that check is included in the visit. A reassuring reading is not a whole-home health guarantee. An unusual reading also needs interpretation before it becomes a diagnosis, a safety claim or a reason to buy equipment.

sections.heading: Choose an action you can judge against the original concern
sections.body: Before choosing a product or visit, ask what the action is intended to address, what it includes and what would still need checking afterward. Keep the original room, timing and observation available so the later discussion does not begin again with a generic indoor-air label. A health symptom needs an appropriate healthcare conversation; an air cleaner is not medical treatment. For a service inquiry, share the concern and address, then confirm assessment scope, charges, coverage and availability. A request is not a confirmed appointment. The useful first result may be a clearer question or a referral need rather than an equipment purchase.

sections.heading: Compare a proposed action with a specific concern
sections.body: Imagine a hypothetical homeowner asking about dust in one room and a smell in another. Keep two lines in the concern record. Ask what a proposed particle filter is intended to address and whether the odor needs a different check. Add the location, timing, possible source and any measurement to the appropriate line without treating them as confirmed causes. If a product is proposed, record its target, room or system fit, care needs and limits beside that concern. This avoids treating one device as evidence that both questions have been answered. The record can also show that an issue remains outside the visit’s scope. A clearer question is a useful outcome even before a product or further investigation is chosen.

faqs.question: Does a particle filter remove gases too?
faqs.answer: A particle filter targets airborne particles. Gas removal uses different filtering material and has its own limits. Match the product to a named concern.

faqs.question: Can an air cleaner guarantee a health result?
faqs.answer: No. Air-cleaning performance is limited by the pollutant, airflow, room conditions and product. A device is not a medical diagnosis or treatment.

ST-080.title: Repair or replace your air conditioner?
ST-080.summary: Start with the cause, the condition and what each option would change. Compare a complete repair with a complete replacement project.
ST-080.answer: An AC symptom or age alone does not settle the choice. Find the cause, then compare repair scope, parts, condition and the full replacement work.

sections.heading: Start with the cooling problem you want to solve
sections.body: The house is warm, the AC stopped again or a repair quote has you wondering about a new system. Start with that concern. Write one sentence about what changed, which rooms are affected and when it happens. “The upstairs stays warm each afternoon” is a different question from “the whole house stopped cooling yesterday.” Neither description proves that replacement is needed. Keep the original concern beside the options so you can ask what each one would address. If the system still works and you are planning ahead, say that too. A planned comparison and a current failure can need different next steps.

sections.heading: Ask what supports the diagnosis
sections.body: Before comparing prices, ask what was checked and what the results showed. Warm air, ice and water can have different causes. Restricted airflow or a refrigerant problem can both lead to ice on the indoor coil. The same symptom does not establish the same repair in every home. If ice appears, stop cooling and arrange a qualified assessment; thawing alone does not explain the cause. Do not open electrical panels, repeatedly reset a tripping breaker or try to add refrigerant. A useful explanation separates the confirmed finding, the possible contributors and anything that still needs checking.

sections.heading: Make the repair option clear
sections.body: Ask exactly what the proposed repair includes and what it is expected to restore. Which component or problem is being addressed? Are the needed parts available? Is further investigation required before a complete price is known? Check the actual equipment warranty and the proposed repair terms rather than assuming that every part or return visit is covered. Keep those questions with the written repair scope. If the issue has happened before, share the past service record if available. A recurring problem deserves an explanation, but the number of visits alone does not tell you whether repair or replacement is the sound choice.

sections.heading: Refrigerant type is one factor, not a replacement order
sections.body: If the air conditioner uses R-22, ask how that affects the actual repair. EPA says the phaseout alone does not require replacing or converting an existing R-22 system. That does not promise that a repair will be practical: refrigerant availability, the location and extent of a leak, parts, condition and cost still matter. Ask which of those factors was checked. Keep refrigerant handling with a qualified technician. Do not treat a refrigerant label as proof that an otherwise unexplained replacement recommendation is necessary, or as proof that keeping the old system must be the better choice.

sections.heading: Compare a complete replacement system
sections.body: An outdoor unit is only part of a replacement proposal. Ask which indoor equipment is matched with it, which furnace and fan remain and whether controls or wiring change. The appropriate cooling capacity should follow the home’s cooling needs and the model’s performance data. ACCA’s Manual S describes equipment selection using home loads and design conditions. Ask how the proposal applies that reasoning to your home. A larger unit is not automatically the answer to a hot room. Keep the room concern visible and ask which checks support the proposed size and what remains outside the replacement scope.

sections.heading: Keep efficiency separate from a savings promise
sections.body: SEER2 is a cooling efficiency rating under a test method. It helps compare equipment, but it does not predict the bill at your home. Equipment fit, actual use, energy prices and the home itself affect running cost. If you receive a cost estimate, ask which assumptions it uses and how uncertainty is shown. Do not compare an old SEER number with SEER2 as though the test methods were identical. A higher advertised rating does not establish a fixed savings amount or payback date. Ask for the rating of the exact proposed equipment combination, not only an “up to” figure.

sections.heading: Put both options on the same page
sections.body: Place the full repair scope beside the full replacement scope. For each, note the price, excluded work, open costs, parts or equipment availability and what concern the option is expected to address. Ask who arranges any permits, electrical work and final inspection, and whether those items are included. Keep possible incentives separate from confirmed reductions and the amount due. Financing has separate approval, repayment and cost terms. A monthly payment is not the project price. If one proposal leaves work to another trade, clarify the responsibility and cost before treating its total as directly comparable with another proposal.

sections.heading: Age and past repairs help describe the situation
sections.body: An older system can still have a repair worth considering, and a newer system can have a problem that deserves a careful assessment. Avoid a birthday rule or a fixed repair-price percentage as the whole decision. Ask what the current condition, repair history and available support mean for these particular choices. In a hypothetical example, a control repair that restores cooling and a replacement intended to address an ongoing room complaint are not yet equivalent options. Ask whether they answer the same question. That example is a comparison aid, not an MGI customer story or evidence of a predicted result.

sections.heading: Choose the next useful step
sections.body: You may have enough information to authorize a supported repair, compare a complete replacement, seek a second assessment or wait for a missing answer. Ask what could change the recommendation and which question needs an answer before you decide. If replacement is the chosen path, ask about startup checks, control guidance and who owns any unfinished item. If you need a visit, share the address, main concern and any useful past work record. Confirm the available service, assessment scope, charges and scheduling. A request does not confirm an appointment, and general guidance does not diagnose your air conditioner.

faqs.question: Does an older AC have to be replaced?
faqs.answer: No universal age rule decides the answer. The actual finding, condition, parts support, home needs and full costs matter.

faqs.question: Does R-22 mean replacement is required?
faqs.answer: EPA says the phaseout alone does not require replacing or converting an existing R-22 system. Actual repair feasibility, refrigerant availability and cost still need checking.

faqs.question: Can a new AC fix a hot room?
faqs.answer: It may address a supported equipment problem, but a room complaint alone does not establish that replacement or a larger unit is the answer. Ask what the assessment explains.

ST-081.title: Repair or replace your water heater?
ST-081.summary: No hot water or a leak does not tell the whole story. Compare the finding, tank condition, hot-water delivery and complete installation scope.
ST-081.answer: Identify why hot water changed or where a leak starts. Then compare a supported repair with replacement that fits the home’s hot-water needs and installation requirements.

sections.heading: Begin with what changed at the tap
sections.body: No hot water, shorter showers or water near the heater can all start a repair-or-replace question. Write down what changed and whether it affects every fixture or only one. Note whether the problem appeared suddenly or has become more noticeable over time. You do not need to know the failed part before asking for help. For a gas smell or suspected carbon-monoxide emergency, leave and contact emergency services or the gas utility from safety. Do not wait for an equipment request. For a hot-water problem without immediate danger, use the observations to start an assessment of the actual heater.

sections.heading: Distinguish the symptom from the cause
sections.body: A water heater that provides less hot water does not automatically have a failed tank. On some electric tanks with two heating elements, a failed element can reduce available hot water. Controls, fuel or power and the household’s hot-water use can also affect the conversation. Ask which checks establish the problem for the actual model. Keep internal electrical, burner and gas work with a qualified person. Do not change settings or open equipment to test a guess. A useful finding explains what was checked, what was found and why the proposed work addresses the reported symptom.

sections.heading: A wet area needs its own explanation
sections.body: Water near a heater can come from a fitting, the temperature-and-pressure relief device or the tank itself. Those findings can lead to different choices. Ask where the moisture starts and what evidence distinguishes the source. The relief device has a protective discharge role; do not plug its outlet or treat discharge as something to hide. A wet floor alone cannot tell you whether a connection can be repaired or the tank condition supports replacement. Describe the location and timing without reaching into the equipment. Let a qualified assessment explain the leak and the appropriate work before comparing options.

sections.heading: Understand what a repair would change
sections.body: Ask for the specific repair scope, parts availability and any questions that remain open. What would the work restore, and how would its result be checked? Which actual warranty or service terms apply? Do not assume a parts warranty includes every labor charge or that a repair includes unrelated work. If the concern has returned, share the earlier record and ask whether the current finding explains the recurrence. Repair may be a useful option when the cause and condition support it. Replacement may deserve comparison when they do not. Neither conclusion follows from the word “leak” or the heater’s age alone.

sections.heading: Match replacement delivery to the busiest use
sections.body: For a conventional storage water heater, tank volume tells you only part of the delivery story. First-hour rating estimates the hot water delivered in the first hour when the tank begins fully heated. Compare that information with when the household uses hot water: showers close together, laundry or other overlapping needs. Ask how the proposed model’s delivery fits that pattern. A larger tank is not automatically the right answer, and a repeated shortage is not proof that size alone caused it. Fuel, recovery, space and the findings on the existing heater belong in the comparison too.

sections.heading: Compare the whole installation job
sections.body: Ask what removal, new equipment, connections and final checks are included in the proposal. If fuel, electrical supply, venting or the installation location changes, clarify the additional work and who performs it. Define permit and inspection responsibilities and any costs left outside the quote. An unexplained “by others” note leaves an important question open. Ask what must happen before the heater can be installed and which owner confirms completion. Identifying a plumbing or electrical dependency does not establish that MGI offers general plumbing or every trade. The actual service scope and project agreement must define the supported work.

sections.heading: Treat efficiency and alternatives as separate questions
sections.body: Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, is a water-heater efficiency measure. Compare equipment using the appropriate product and hot-water-use categories; the rating is not a guarantee of a household bill. Fuel prices, use and installation conditions matter when comparing operating costs. If someone proposes a tankless or heat-pump water heater instead of a conventional tank, ask for a separate fit and project comparison. Different technologies can have different space, power, drainage and care requirements. Do not assume that a technology label, incentive possibility or efficiency figure proves it fits the home or that MGI supports every model.

sections.heading: Use condition, records and costs together
sections.body: Gather the model information and service history if you have them. The equipment’s age helps describe the situation but cannot replace a condition check. Put the full repair beside the full replacement project, including exclusions and unresolved costs. Keep financing, any possible incentive and the amount due as separate items until the actual terms are confirmed. A cheaper monthly payment is not necessarily a smaller total commitment. Ask which findings make repair viable, which support replacement and what would change the answer. You can request clarification before choosing, without relying on a universal age limit or repair-price rule.

sections.heading: Leave with a clear decision and owner
sections.body: The next useful step may be a supported repair, a replacement assessment or an answer about an unresolved leak or installation dependency. Ask what needs attention now and what can be planned later. Before authorizing installation, ask about the actual model’s controls, appropriate temperature guidance, care instructions and operating checks. Water temperature has safety implications; use qualified advice for the system rather than a generic setting as a personal prescription. For a service inquiry, describe the concern and address, then confirm scope, charges and availability. An inquiry is not an appointment. Keep the findings and agreement so the result can be compared with the original hot-water concern.

faqs.question: Does no hot water mean I need a new tank?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Controls, fuel or power, heating parts and demand can matter. A qualified assessment should establish the cause.

faqs.question: Is every water-heater leak a failed tank?
faqs.answer: No. Moisture can come from connections, a relief device or the tank. The source needs checking before choosing a repair or replacement.

faqs.question: Should I buy the same tank size again?
faqs.answer: Compare hot-water use and first-hour delivery as well as tank volume. The existing size alone does not prove the next model will meet the household’s needs.
