BLOG-MANUAL-J.title: What is a Manual J Calculation and Why is It Important?
BLOG-MANUAL-J.summary: A load calculation helps explain how much heating and cooling your home needs. Learn what to ask before choosing replacement equipment.
BLOG-MANUAL-J.answer: Manual J is a method for estimating a home’s heating and cooling needs. That calculation helps guide equipment selection. It is more useful than choosing a new system only from the size of the old one or the home’s square footage.

sections.heading: Start with your home, then choose the equipment.
sections.body: A replacement quote should help you understand why a system fits. Begin with the home you have now, not just the unit being removed. Tell the person preparing the proposal about rooms that are hard to heat or cool, recent work on the house, and changes you are planning. Keep those observations separate from a diagnosis. A room that feels uncomfortable does not, by itself, prove that the main equipment is too small. Ask what information supports the recommendation and which questions still need a closer look. Make a short list of the issues you want the proposed work to address.

sections.heading: What does Manual J calculate?
sections.body: ACCA, the Air Conditioning Contractors of America, publishes Manual J for residential load calculations. The method accounts for how a home gains and loses heat. Inputs include building surfaces, windows, air leakage, ventilation, duct effects, and selected indoor and outdoor conditions. A calculation can describe the whole home and individual rooms. It is a design tool, not a measurement of next month’s bill. The result depends on the information entered. Ask whether the report reflects your actual home and what was assumed where a detail could not be checked. Keep the report with your equipment records so that later discussions have the same starting point.

sections.heading: Give the assessment a useful starting point.
sections.body: You do not need to create a technical report before asking for help. A short written record is enough to start the conversation. Note which rooms feel different, when the issue shows up, and whether it changed after work on the home. Gather records you already have instead of guessing at hidden construction details. Say when a detail is unknown. That lets the person doing the assessment identify what needs confirmation. Avoid entering attics, opening equipment, or taking risks to collect information for a quote. The assessment should fill in technical gaps rather than depend on you to investigate them.
bullets: List window, insulation, or air-sealing work you know about.
Describe any finished space or changed room use.
Keep available equipment records and earlier proposals together.
Write down the comfort questions you want the proposal to answer.

sections.heading: Ask how the room-by-room picture affects the plan.
sections.body: A single total does not tell the whole story of how air reaches each room. If one room is the reason you are considering work, make that clear before selecting equipment. Ask how the proposed plan addresses that room and what remains outside the work. A useful discussion may include delivery of air as well as equipment capacity. Do not assume a larger unit will resolve every uneven room. Ask the contractor to connect the recommendation to the assessment, then explain which parts of the proposed work address the concern you actually reported. Put any unresolved room concerns into the written discussion.

sections.heading: Manual J, Manual S, and Manual D have different jobs.
sections.body: Manual J estimates the load. ACCA’s Manual S addresses equipment selection, using the load and equipment performance information. Manual D addresses residential duct design. These are connected tasks, but they are not interchangeable reports. A load calculation does not select a model on its own or show that existing ducts suit every replacement choice. When comparing proposals, ask how the equipment was selected and how the air-distribution plan was considered. You are looking for an explanation of the whole proposed system, not simply three manual names printed on a quote. Ask the person preparing it to explain unfamiliar terms in everyday language.

sections.heading: Compare the reasoning behind different recommendations.
sections.body: Two proposals may recommend different equipment. Start by asking each contractor to explain the inputs, the selected equipment, and the work included. Keep a copy of the calculation or summary they agree to provide. Ask about any difference in the treatment of rooms, planned home changes, or existing ducts. A lower price and a larger model are both incomplete comparisons without that context. If an explanation is unclear, ask for it in plain language. You can pause the decision while an open question is resolved rather than choosing from model numbers alone. Make sure both proposals address the same intended outcome.

sections.heading: Separate the calculation from the quote.
sections.body: Confirm what the proposed assessment includes, whether it has a charge, and what documents you will receive. Then compare the installation scope separately. Ask who handles any required electrical, duct, control, permit, or other work and whether it is included in the price. Get exclusions in writing. A calculation does not establish a project’s final cost, rebate eligibility, or completion date. Those questions need their own answers. This helps you see what you are buying and who is responsible for each part before you approve the work. Keep any agreed changes with the final proposal rather than only in conversation.

sections.heading: Use the findings to make a clear next choice.
sections.body: Bring the conversation back to the needs of your home. Ask why the recommended system fits, how the proposal addresses the concern that brought you here, and what could change the recommendation. Keep unresolved items visible in the written plan. If home improvements are still being planned, explain that before the selection is final. The goal is a supported equipment decision with a clear scope. Ask MGI about replacement planning for your existing home and confirm the assessment, visit terms, and next step before arranging work. A useful plan gives you enough information to choose without promising a particular bill or perfect temperature.

faqs.question: Can I choose replacement equipment from square footage alone?
faqs.answer: Square footage is one input. Ask for a home-specific assessment and the reasoning behind equipment selection rather than relying on area alone.

faqs.question: Does a Manual J calculation guarantee lower bills?
faqs.answer: No. A load calculation supports design. It does not promise a particular bill, temperature, or savings result.

MIGRATION-FAQ.title: Questions about working with MGI.
MIGRATION-FAQ.summary: Start here for service requests, appointments, and where to find help.
MIGRATION-FAQ.answer: Ask about service online or by phone. MGI must confirm your address, availability, and appointment details.

sections.heading: How do I ask about service?
sections.body: Open Schedule service to use the ServiceTitan scheduler, or call MGI at (970) 287-1673. Have your address and the main problem ready.

sections.heading: Is my request a confirmed appointment?
sections.body: No. The scheduler says an appointment is pending confirmation. Check the visit details with MGI before treating a time as confirmed.

sections.heading: Does MGI serve my address?
sections.body: Contact MGI to confirm service at your address and current availability. A town page does not confirm an appointment or availability at every address.

sections.heading: Where can I find equipment answers?
sections.body: Visit Homeowner help for heating, cooling, and water-heating guides. The guides explain common questions. They do not replace a qualified check of your equipment.

sections.heading: How do I check prices, financing, or rebates?
sections.body: Ask MGI about the work and its price. Financing and rebate eligibility depend on the current program rules and your project. Confirm the terms before counting a benefit.
